source.title_on_document: When LLMs meet creativity: rethinking GFL writing through Human–LLM co-creation

paper_design_summary: A controlled experiment compared human-only writing, human–LLM collaborative writing, and LLM-only writing. Forty Chinese undergraduate students of German as a foreign language each completed four writing tasks under their assigned conditions, and the writings were evaluated on a Torrance-inspired rubric covering fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration. The abstract does not specify the assignment method, assignment unit, design structure, or arm sizes.

eligibility.reason: Abstract only; full text was not obtained. The abstract reports 40 participating students, so at most 40 people were analyzed, below the 50-person threshold (OpenAlex W7162853600, abstract, sentence 4). Random assignment, assignment unit, design structure, arm sizes, and exclusions are not stated (sentences 3–4 and complete abstract). The writings were evaluated with a Torrance-inspired rubric covering fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration (sentence 5). The human-only versus LLM-only output comparison supports AI-versus-human context (sentences 3 and 7–8). List in the screening report as a small experiment.

one_line_finding: In a controlled experiment with 40 Chinese GFL undergraduates, human–LLM collaborative writing had the highest creativity scores, particularly in elaboration and originality, human-only writing showed comparable originality to collaborative writing, and LLM-only writing had the lowest overall creativity scores; the abstract reports no numerical outcome statistics (OpenAlex W7162853600, abstract, sentences 4–8).

audit_corrections.basis: The abstract reports human-only, human-LLM, and LLM-only writing scored on one rubric; the core criteria fail (40 people, assignment not stated), and the human-only versus LLM-only comparison is AI-versus-human context.
